insights.insight: $2.55M in cryptographically confirmed GMV across 36,822 receipts establishes a live, deterministic purchase dataset — not modeled, not inferred. At ~370–380 receipts per day with no decay, this is a stable signal base, not a spike artifact.

Grocery leads receipt volume (1,287 receipts, ~$61 avg basket) but restaurants compress average ticket to ~$37; an unclassified 'Unknown' category runs ~$338/receipt — roughly 5.5x grocery — and its count is edging up, suggesting high-ticket purchase behavior that warrants category resolution before media planning.

The industry pays $5+ CPM to infer purchase intent from browsing signals; a verified receipt is a closed-loop confirmation that a transaction occurred at a named merchant. The structural value of that gap compounds as third-party cookie deprecation removes the probabilistic layer entirely.

Walmart (360 receipts), Costco (165), Target (113), Kroger (80), and The Home Depot (77) account for a disproportionate share of confirmed 14-day purchase activity — useful for benchmarking competitive share-of-wallet and identifying switching behavior at the receipt level.

Four consecutive UTC midnight rollovers produced mechanical GMV drops of 15–35% that fully recovered within four hours each time — confirming the throughput signal is structurally stable and that short-window reads taken before noon should be treated as provisional, not directional.

insights.topic: Category mix shift compressing average basket
insights.insight: Average basket has compressed from prior ~$80 readings to ~$65.57 on the 14-day window and ~$54.70 on the 7-day — driven by grocery and dining gaining receipt share, not by demand softening. CMOs benchmarking against older basket figures should adjust for category mix before drawing performance conclusions.
